text.text: Every dish should be costed before it goes on the menu, and again whenever a main ingredient's price moves. Costing from the recipe makes that automatic.
Weigh the real portion as it goes on the plate, not the recipe card's guess.
Add one recipe line per ingredient that matters: the protein, the starch, the sauce base, the expensive garnish.
Enter the amount in the same unit the ingredient is counted in. If bass is counted in pounds, a 7-ounce portion is 0.44.
Put oil, salt, pepper, herbs and trim into the

Many ingredients lose weight in trimming and cooking. A whole fish yields maybe 45 percent as fillet; a pork shoulder loses a third in the braise. Cost on the trimmed amount, or include the loss in the amount per plate.
Food cost percent is not the whole story. A steak at 38 percent can make more dollars per plate than a salad at 22 percent. Look at
together: popular dishes with a good margin are the ones to protect.
Supplier price change of 5 percent or more on a main ingredient
Every three months for every dish, even if nothing seems to change
. Cost them before the first tasting, not after the menu is printed.
The smoked trout toast tests at 15 dollars with a recipe cost of about 4.30. The chef is happy with the food cost but asks for a thicker slice of bread, which adds 20 cents per plate.
Counting is how a kitchen finds money it is losing. Count the same way, at the same time, every week.
Count Monday morning before deliveries, or Sunday night after close.
Walk the same route each week: walk-in, reach-ins, freezer, dry storage, bar, paper.
Count in the unit on the sheet (pounds, cases, bottles). Partial cases count in tenths.
Par is the amount you need to get from one delivery to the next, plus a little cushion.

cells.text: Two nights of sales; deliveries Wednesday and Friday

text.text: Review pars every month. A par that is always overstocked ties up money and goes to waste.

Cost of goods used is the opening inventory value, plus purchases, minus the closing inventory value. Divide it by food sales for the week. If it is much higher than the menu's average food cost, the gap is waste, over-portioning, theft or comps.
First in, first out: new deliveries go behind older stock.
Label and date everything that is opened or prepped.
Turn what is close to its date into a special or staff meal.
Write down what is thrown out and why.
The same two people count every week, one calling and one writing, so the numbers are comparable. The chef spot-checks five expensive items each week, such as fish, steak and spirits.
Prepped items counted on the prep list, not here
Anything damaged or spoiled written off with a note
Striped bass is at 9 pounds against a par of 18, so it is flagged for the Wednesday fish order. Arborio is above par, so dry goods can skip it this week.
Ordering on a schedule keeps the walk-in full but not overflowing, and makes delivery minimums easy to meet.
Open Inventory and filter to the supplier. Items flagged Order show
Adjust for the week ahead: a holiday, a private party, a menu change.
Make sure the order meets the supplier's
Draft the order with the delivery date; send it and set
Check every item against the order and the invoice
Temperatures: chilled food at 41 degrees Fahrenheit or below, frozen solid
Quality: reject soft fish, wilted greens, damaged cases
Weigh proteins that are sold by weight
Note shorts and substitutions on the invoice before the driver leaves
Put away cold food first, then dry goods
with the date, and update costs on Inventory if prices changed.
When an order is late or short

A Sent order whose delivery date has passed shows under Overdue. Call the supplier before service, decide what to 86 or substitute, and tell the floor team at line-up. Note the miss on the supplier's page; a supplier who is short three times in a month gets compared with the backup.
Pay on time; it is the best way to get the best product when supply is short.
Ask for price lists every month and compare two suppliers on your top ten items twice a year.
Keep one backup supplier for each category.
The weekend fish order is still a draft for Friday's delivery. The chef adds two extra pounds of bass for a party of twelve on Saturday and sends it before the Wednesday cut-off.
Opening and closing the same way every day protects the food, the building and the inspection score.
Walk-in, reach-ins and freezer temperatures logged
Hand sinks stocked with soap and towels; sanitizer buckets at the right strength
Floor: tables set, restrooms checked, menus clean
Food covered, labeled, dated and put away
Hot food cooled correctly before going in the walk-in
Equipment off; hood filters cleaned on schedule
Floors swept and mopped; trash and recycling out
On-hand counts entered for the next prep list

Twice a day, write the temperature of every cooler and freezer. Coolers hold 41 degrees Fahrenheit or below, freezers 0 or below. A cooler reading high twice in a row is moved to the backup cooler and a repair is called the same day. Inspectors ask to see this log.
Inspections are easier when every day looks like inspection day.

text.text: Log it with the date, score and findings.
Fix, photograph the fix, and set
Talk through the findings at the next staff meeting, so the whole team knows what the inspector saw and why it matters.
The monthly self-inspection found a torn walk-in door gasket and two unlabeled containers. Labels were fixed on the spot; the gasket is ordered and due to be fitted before the fix-by date.

A restaurant makes or loses money in small amounts: a few cents a plate, an hour of overtime, a case of herbs thrown out. This workspace puts those numbers where the chef and the owner see them every week.

Striped bass went up a dollar a pound. The chef updates the cost on Inventory, sees the bass dish move from 35 to 36 percent food cost, and trims the portion slightly rather than raise the price mid-season.
A good prep list means service starts calm. It says what each station makes, how much, and who makes it.
For each station, list what must be ready before service: sauces, portioned proteins, pickles, doughs, garnishes.
for a normal night in the unit you prep in (quarts, portions, pans).

Busy nights get a higher par; slow nights a lower one. Change pars on the list, not in people's heads.

text.text: The sous chef owns the list and changes pars; cooks own their items. When something runs out during service, the cook tells the sous chef, and the par goes up for the next night. Two nights in a row with leftovers means the par goes down.
